rationale: T1589 describes adversary methods for collecting identity information (names, emails, credentials, MFA configurations) through phishing, open-source research, and probing authentication services. Like T1592, the technique describes collection tradecraft rather than targeting a specific client asset a defender can fabricate. The dominant collection vectors remain outside defender control. The authentication probing edge case maps more cleanly to active scanning or credential access techniques than to this parent technique as defined.

T1590 describes collection tradecraft targeting network information (IP ranges, domain names, DNS, topology, trust dependencies, security appliances) through active scanning, phishing, and open technical databases. Active scanning is already evaluated under T1595. The remaining vectors are outside defender control. Individual sub-techniques may be evaluated separately where specific defender-controlled assets are involved.

T1591 covers collection of organizational intelligence (divisions, business operations, key roles, physical locations, business relationships) through phishing, social media, and open-source research. No defender-controlled asset can be fabricated to intercept this collection. Planting false organizational information as deception crosses into infoops territory rather than deploying a decoy client asset, which is outside the scope of this matrix.

T1592 describes adversary methods for collecting host information rather than targeting a specific client asset. Active scanning is already evaluated under T1595. The remaining collection vectors (phishing for information, compromised third-party sites, open-source data collection) either target people rather than infrastructure or fall outside defender control entirely. There is no coherent decoy asset a defender can fabricate that maps to this technique as a whole.

The parent technique is dominated by passive open-source collection (social media, search engines, general web searches) outside defender control. However, T1593.003 (Code Repositories) supports a decoy asset model via a self-hosted repository (e.g., GitLab) containing honeytoken credentials or decoy configuration files — a technical entity on defender-controlled infrastructure. Interaction is Mostly No because discovery depends on attackers finding the repository first, which is not guaranteed. Intelligence yield is high when interaction occurs: source IPs, tooling, accessed files, and downstream honeytoken use. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because a publicly exposed repository could be accessed by researchers or crawlers, though cloning or using honeytoken content is unambiguously malicious.

A decoy website (fake corporate portal, intranet login page, or department site) is a technical entity on defender-controlled infrastructure that sits directly in the path of this technique. Interaction is Mostly Yes because the decoy must first be discoverable via search engines, DNS, or OSINT. Intelligence yield is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because public-facing websites attract significant noise (crawlers, bots, scanners) that reduces effective signal. Malice fidelity is Mostly No for the same reason: distinguishing malicious reconnaissance from benign browsing requires heavy correlation with other data sources, as there is no inherent expectation of no legitimate access to a public website.

A wide range of client assets can be mimicked as decoys across all three sub-techniques (IP block scanning, vulnerability scanning, wordlist scanning): live hosts, open ports and services, web servers, databases, VPN endpoints, OT/ICS interfaces, and more. Active scanning is largely indiscriminate, so decoy assets in exposed IP space will be probed just like real assets. Interaction yields actionable intelligence including source IPs, tool signatures (nmap, Masscan, Shodan), targeted ports and services, and wordlists. Malice fidelity is high by the honeypot definition: no legitimate party has reason to probe a fabricated asset.

T1596 involves passive querying of third-party databases (DNS/passive DNS, WHOIS, certificate transparency logs, CDNs, scan databases such as Shodan and Censys). While the data in these databases originates from defender-controlled infrastructure, the adversary interacts with third-party services the defender does not control or monitor. There is no observable interaction with a fabricated client asset. Planting fake data to appear in these databases is outside scope (infoops).

T1597 is entirely passive collection from external commercial or criminal databases (threat intel vendors, dark web markets). The adversary never touches defender-controlled infrastructure. There is no technical entity a defender can fabricate and place in the path of that collection. Seeding fake data into threat intel feeds or dark web markets would constitute infoops and is outside scope.

Scoped to server-side technical phishing traps only: decoy mailboxes and decoy credential honeytokens. These are technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure. Planting false data in external breach databases or paste sites is outside scope (infoops). Interaction is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because attackers must first discover and harvest the decoy asset before phishing it — that discovery step is not guaranteed. Once interaction occurs, intelligence yield is high: attacker infrastructure, phishing kit fingerprints, lure content, and targeting patterns. Malice fidelity is high since no legitimate party has reason to phish a fabricated mailbox or submit a honeytoken credential.

T1681 describes adversaries monitoring threat intelligence sources for reporting on their own operations. The technique is entirely self-referential from the adversary's perspective: they query third-party platforms about their own infrastructure, not interacting with anything on the defender's side. No fabricated client asset applies.

T1583 describes adversaries acquiring their own operational infrastructure (servers, domains, DNS, botnets, web services). The technique is entirely about the adversary's own resource acquisition process on their side. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate or place in the path of an adversary registering a domain or renting a VPS.

T1584 describes adversaries compromising third-party infrastructure (servers, domains, network devices, botnets) for use as operational platforms. The defender is not the target; the compromised infrastructure belongs to third parties. The technique is entirely adversary-side resource preparation with no interaction with defender-controlled assets.

T1585 describes adversaries creating and cultivating accounts and personas (social media, email, cloud) on third-party platforms. The process is entirely adversary-side with no interaction with defender-controlled infrastructure. Creating a fake persona to monitor adversary activity would constitute active counterintelligence, not deploying a decoy client asset, and is outside scope.

T1586 describes adversaries compromising existing accounts (social media, email, cloud) through credential theft, purchasing, brute force, or insider access. The technique is about the adversary's account acquisition process, not interaction with defender-controlled infrastructure. A honeypot account with exposed credentials would require seeding in external breach databases or paste sites, which crosses into infoops territory and is outside the scope of this matrix.

T1587 is entirely adversary-side capability development — building malware, exploits, code signing certificates, and digital certificates in their own environment. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate that sits in the path of an adversary writing code or generating a certificate. The technique has no interaction with defender-controlled infrastructure by definition.

T1588 describes adversaries purchasing, downloading, or stealing capabilities (malware, tools, exploits, certificates, vulnerability data) from third-party sources and criminal marketplaces. Same pattern as T1587: entirely adversary-side capability acquisition with no interaction with defender-controlled infrastructure.

T1608 describes adversaries staging their own capabilities (malware, tools, phishing pages, certificates) on infrastructure they control. The technique is entirely adversary-side preparation with no interaction with defender-controlled infrastructure.

T1650 describes adversaries purchasing existing access from initial access brokers — transactions that occur entirely in criminal marketplaces between the adversary and a third party. The defender has no asset to fabricate here; the technique does not involve the adversary interacting with defender-controlled infrastructure. Creating a fake compromised system listing on an IAB marketplace would constitute an offensive counterintelligence operation, outside the scope of this matrix.

Decoy accounts (honey accounts, honeytoken credentials, decoy SSH keys, fake service accounts) are fabricated technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure — AD, cloud IAM, SSH authorized_keys — that are passive and fully instrumented. Feasibility is Yes: the asset is well-established in practice and straightforward to deploy. Interaction is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the decoy credential must first be acquired before it can be used; interaction depends on placement strategy (breadcrumb in a config file, exposed in a compromised endpoint) rather than being self-attracting like a public-facing service. Intelligence yield is high: authentication metadata, source IP, timing patterns, targeted service, and post-authentication behavior if the account grants access to a decoy environment. Malice fidelity is Yes: no legitimate user knows about or has reason to use a fabricated account; false positives are limited to controlled security testing scenarios and are operationally manageable.

T1091 requires physical media to be inserted into a system — the adversary introduces the attack vector rather than targeting a specific defender-controlled asset. Similar to T1200, the attacker brings the vector into the environment. A decoy endpoint configured to detect USB insertions is endpoint detection, not a fabricated client asset that attracts or intercepts the adversary.

Decoy remote access services (fake VPN endpoints, honeypot RDP/SSH servers, fake OWA portals, exposed Docker/Kubernetes APIs) are technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure that sit directly in the path of this technique. Exposed remote services are hit constantly by opportunistic brute-forcers and credential stuffers without requiring prior discovery. Intelligence yield is high: credential sets in circulation, brute force tooling, password spray patterns, and post-authentication attacker behavior. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes due to asset-type variance — generic SSH/RDP endpoints attract scanner noise, while internal-looking or specialized services (fake OWA, decoy VPN) have higher signal.

T1189 targets visiting client browsers, not a specific server asset the defender controls as a decoy target. The adversary sets up or compromises a website to exploit browsers that visit it. The defender's endpoints are the victims, not something that can be fabricated to attract and intercept the adversary. A decoy website that detects compromise attempts maps to T1584 (Compromise Infrastructure), not T1189.

A wide range of internet-facing assets can be fabricated as decoys: web servers, VPN appliances, mail servers, databases, network devices, SSH endpoints, and cloud management interfaces. Internet-facing services are probed constantly — opportunistically by automated scanners and targeted by adversaries seeking specific vulnerable software — so a realistic decoy attracts interaction without requiring prior discovery. Intelligence yield is high: exploit payloads, CVEs targeted, tool signatures, and post-exploitation behavior. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because fidelity varies by asset type: generic web servers attract significant noise from scanners and researchers, while specialized appliances (VPN endpoints, Exchange, ESXi) and internal-looking services have much higher signal.

T1195 targets the supply chain upstream of the defender — development tools, source repositories, software update channels, open-source dependencies, and hardware before it reaches the consumer. The adversary compromises components the defender will later consume, not a specific asset the defender currently controls and can fabricate as a decoy. By the time the defender receives the compromised product, the attack has already succeeded. A decoy software update channel or hardware shipment would require active counterintelligence operations outside the scope of this matrix.

T1199 operates through third-party compromise: the adversary breaches an MSP, contractor, or cloud reseller that already has legitimate access to the target, then pivots through that existing trust relationship. The attack has two stages — compromising the third party (outside defender control) and using their access to reach the victim. A defender could theoretically create a decoy environment accessible via third-party credentials, but it would not naturally attract adversaries: for interaction to occur, a specific third party with access to the decoy would first need to be compromised, a chain the defender cannot influence or predict. The trusted relationship is not a client asset the defender can fabricate and place in the path of this technique.

T1200 is adversary-initiated physical insertion — the attacker brings hardware into the defender's environment rather than targeting a specific asset the defender controls. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate that sits in the path of someone physically connecting a rogue device. A decoy network port designed to detect unauthorized connections would require physical security infrastructure and falls outside the infrastructure deception model of this matrix.

Scoped to decoy mailboxes on defender-controlled mail infrastructure — passive technical assets that receive, log, and alert on phishing attempts. Active accounts that click links or open attachments are puppets, not decoys, and are out of scope. Interaction is Mostly Yes because the decoy address must first be harvested before it gets phished, though phishing campaigns are high volume and addresses leak through many channels. Intelligence yield is high and stronger than T1598: sending infrastructure, malware samples or exploit documents, phishing kit fingerprints, C2 links, and campaign tooling. Malice fidelity is Yes — no legitimate party sends malicious payloads to a fabricated mailbox; noise is rare and distinguishable.

T1659 targets network traffic in transit — adversaries inject content from the middle (ISP-level) or from the side (racing fake responses). The technique does not target a specific client asset a defender can fabricate. A decoy client could potentially detect injection attacks but cannot lure or intercept the adversary in any intelligence-generating way; the adversary targets traffic flows, not specific assets.

A decoy Wi-Fi access point mimicking a corporate secured network is a technical entity on defender-controlled infrastructure that sits directly in the path of this technique. Feasibility is Yes: decoy APs are well-established and straightforward to instrument. Interaction is Mostly No because T1669 requires physical proximity or prior compromise of a dual-homed system nearby — the decoy is not reachable by internet-wide scanners and interaction depends on adversary proximity, which the defender cannot reliably engineer. Intelligence yield is high when interaction occurs: device identifiers, authentication attempts and credentials, probe request fingerprints, and post-connection tool behavior. Malice fidelity is Yes: a properly named decoy SSID has no prior connection history on legitimate devices, so auto-connect and accidental connection are not plausible; anyone connecting to a fabricated corporate AP is doing so deliberately.

A decoy Windows host with WMI enabled (DCOM on port 135, WinRM on 5985/5986) is a fabricatable client asset — a honeypot VM that authentically presents the WMI interface. Interaction is Mostly No because WMI-based lateral movement requires the attacker to have already discovered the host and obtained valid credentials; the decoy is not self-attracting and depends entirely on prior steps the defender cannot engineer. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: executed commands, WQL queries, process creation events, credential reuse, and post-exploitation behavior are all logged. Malice fidelity is Mostly No because WMI is a legitimate Windows administration interface — a decoy host integrated into the network to be discoverable will also receive legitimate management traffic from domain controllers, monitoring agents, SCCM, and backup tools, requiring significant filtering to isolate malicious activity.

T1053 is an action the attacker performs — creating or modifying scheduled tasks (Windows Task Scheduler, cron, systemd timers, container orchestration jobs) on a host they already control. The technique is the mechanism of execution and persistence, not the targeting of a specific asset a defender can fabricate. There is no client asset to place in the path of an attacker creating a scheduled task; the action is performed on infrastructure the attacker already owns.

Feasibility is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because it is uneven across sub-techniques. Decoy network devices (T1059.008), hypervisors (T1059.012), containers (T1059.013), and cloud APIs (T1059.009) are fabricatable client assets with externally accessible CLI or API interfaces that sit directly in the path of this technique. The dominant sub-techniques (PowerShell, bash, cmd, Python) are post-compromise intra-host execution primitives with no fabricatable external asset. Interaction is Mostly No because the attacker must first obtain credentials and discover the target asset before interacting with it via CLI. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: commands executed, credentials used, source IP, session timing, and tool signatures are all loggable. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes — network device and hypervisor CLIs accessed by unknown accounts are high fidelity, while cloud and container sub-techniques may produce FPs from misconfigured automation or CI/CD tooling depending on environment complexity.

Two decoy asset models exist for T1072: a decoy endpoint enrolled in a real deployment system (SCCM, Intune, AWS Systems Manager) that receives malicious deployments pushed broadly by an attacker, or a fake deployment server that lures attackers looking for management platforms to abuse. Feasibility is Mostly No because neither option is clean — the enrolled endpoint is a generic honeypot VM that incidentally receives deployments rather than mimicking the technique specifically, while a convincing fake deployment server is operationally complex to build and maintain. Interaction is Mostly No for the same reasons; the attacker must first compromise the deployment infrastructure and is not specifically targeting the decoy. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the malicious payload, deployment configuration, credential used, and targeting scope are all captured. Malice fidelity is Yes — no legitimate IT process would push deployments to a fabricated asset outside normal inventory.

T1106 involves calling native OS API functions (e.g., `NtCreateProcess`, `CreateProcess`, `fork()`) directly to execute behaviors on a host the attacker already controls. This is an in-process execution mechanism — the technique describes how malware invokes OS functionality, not a method of targeting an external asset. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate and place in the path of this technique.

T1129 is an in-process execution mechanism — the attacker loads shared modules (DLLs on Windows, .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS) into a process they already control using functions like `LoadLibrary` or `dlopen`. The technique targets no external asset; it is a post-compromise action performed entirely within a compromised host. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate and place in the path of this technique.

T1203 exploits vulnerabilities in client-side applications (browsers, Office, PDF readers) by delivering malicious content to the client via phishing or drive-by. The attack is pushed to the client, not pulled toward a server asset the defender controls. This is the client-side mirror of T1190, which targets server assets the defender can deliberately expose. Intercepting T1203 would require an active client honeypot that browses attacker-controlled sites or opens malicious files — a fundamentally different and operationally complex model that does not fit the passive decoy framework of this matrix.

T1204 depends on a human user taking an action — clicking a link, opening a file, pasting and running code. The technique targets user behavior, not a specific client asset a defender can fabricate. There is no infrastructure component to mimic as a decoy; the attack vector is the user themselves. A decoy cannot replicate a human action, and there is no asset to place in the path of this technique.

T1559 covers abusing IPC mechanisms (named pipes, COM/DCOM, DDE, XPC, shared memory) for local code execution within a compromised host. The technique is fundamentally intra-host and post-compromise — the attacker uses IPC to communicate between processes they already control. While sub-technique T1559.001 (COM) can be abused remotely via DCOM, that remote execution angle is already covered under T1047. The parent technique has no external client asset a defender can fabricate and place in the path of an attacker.

T1569 is an execution primitive used on a host the attacker has already compromised — creating or abusing services (Windows SCM, macOS launchctl, Linux systemctl) to run commands. The technique is performed internally after gaining access, not by targeting a specific discoverable asset from outside. There is no client asset a defender can fabricate and place in the path of this technique; the attack surface is the attacker's own post-compromise actions on a host they already control.

A decoy container environment (honeypot Kubernetes cluster or Docker host) is a fabricatable client asset with the administration interface — Docker daemon, Kubernetes API server, kubelet — fully instrumented. Interaction is Mostly Yes because attackers with cluster access typically enumerate all containers broadly (`kubectl get pods --all-namespaces`), making a well-positioned decoy with a plausible name and namespace likely to be discovered and targeted in the same sweep. Intelligence yield is Yes: Kubernetes audit logs and Docker daemon logs capture commands executed, service account or credential used, source IP, and lateral movement patterns within the cluster. Malice fidelity is Yes because the decoy is a purpose-built honeypot cluster with no legitimate workloads — no CI/CD pipelines, orchestration tooling, or real automation has reason to interact with it, so any container execution is definitively malicious.

The primary decoy asset for T1610 is a fabricated container image placed in an internal registry, designed to look like a legitimate base image an attacker might pull to stay stealthy rather than introducing a foreign image. Feasibility is Mostly No because attackers deploying containers typically bring their own images from attacker-controlled registries — the procedure examples show this consistently — so the defender's decoy image sits outside the dominant attack pattern. Interaction is Mostly No for the same reason; a well-crafted deception narrative with a convincingly named image could lure an attacker trying to blend in, but this is operationally difficult and unlikely. Intelligence yield is Yes if interaction occurs: registry pull logs and Kubernetes audit logs capture source IP, credential used, deployment configuration (privileges requested, volumes, network rules), and runtime behavior — a rich signal. Malice fidelity is Yes because a fabricated image with no legitimate operational purpose has no reason to be pulled by real workloads or pipelines; any deployment is definitively malicious.

A decoy serverless function (AWS Lambda, Azure Function, Google Cloud Function) with realistic-looking IAM permissions or planted honeytoken credentials is a fabricatable cloud asset, scoped to the scenario where an attacker abuses an existing function rather than creating their own. Interaction is Mostly No because the attacker must first obtain cloud access before enumerating resources, and interaction probability depends heavily on the deception narrative — a plausible function name and attached roles (e.g., `credential-rotator`, `billing-processor`) are necessary to attract targeting. Intelligence yield is Yes: cloud logs (CloudTrail, Azure Monitor) capture caller identity, IAM role used, source IP, invocation parameters, and any modifications. Malice fidelity is Mostly No because a serverless function visible to anyone with cloud read access may be invoked by curious developers, DevOps engineers, or automation tooling, requiring filtering to isolate malicious invocations from legitimate internal activity.

A decoy cloud VM enrolled in a cloud management service (AWS Systems Manager, Azure RunCommand) is a fabricatable client asset — a honeypot VM registered in the management plane of a decoy or production cloud account. Interaction is Mostly No because the attacker must first obtain cloud administrative access before they can enumerate and target VMs; the decoy is not self-attracting and interaction depends on prior credential compromise. Intelligence yield is Yes: cloud management plane logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log) capture caller identity, source IP, IAM role or credential used, and the exact commands executed — structured, centralised, and tamper-resistant from the VM level. Malice fidelity is Yes: legitimate cloud automation targets specific named or tagged resources; a decoy VM outside normal deployment patterns has no reason to receive management commands, and the noise floor in cloud environments is far lower than in Windows networks with ambient management traffic.

T1674 simulates keystrokes on a victim's system via software (injecting into the Windows message loop) or physical devices (malicious USB HIDs). Both vectors require either a prior foothold on the target system or physical access to it. The technique targets a user session or physical endpoint — there is no client asset a defender can fabricate and place in the path of keystroke injection.

A decoy guest VM hosted on a honeypot ESXi hypervisor is a fabricatable client asset — the attacker uses VMware Tools (`vmtoolsd`, vSphere Web Services SDK) to execute commands on guest VMs from a compromised ESXi host. Interaction is Mostly No because the attacker must first compromise the ESXi host before reaching guest VMs, and even then a decoy VM needs convincing placement among real-looking workloads to be targeted. Intelligence yield is Yes: ESXi and vSphere logs capture API calls (`StartProgramInGuest`, `ListProcessesInGuest`), credentials used, and commands executed; the guest VM itself can be fully instrumented. Malice fidelity is Yes — a fabricated guest VM has no legitimate operational purpose, so no real admin or automation has reason to target it; any VMware Tools-based execution against it is definitively malicious.

The primary decoy asset is a honeypot public repository with a realistic CI/CD pipeline configured with planted honeytoken credentials, targeting the Public Pipeline Execution scenario where attackers submit malicious pull requests from forks to trigger pipelines and leak secrets. Feasibility is Mostly Yes — the asset is buildable but more complex than a simple honeypot VM; the direct and indirect pipeline scenarios require prior repo access and have no natural decoy hook. Interaction is Mostly Yes because automated scanners actively search for repositories with vulnerable pipeline triggers (`pull_request_target`, self-hosted runners), making a well-configured decoy repo self-attracting to a degree. Intelligence yield is Yes: attacker account identity, malicious payload injected, targeted credentials, C2 infrastructure, and full pipeline execution logs are all captured. Malice fidelity is Mostly No because a public repository with a CI/CD pipeline attracts legitimate pull requests, bot activity, dependency update automation, and security researchers, requiring careful filtering to isolate malicious pipeline poisoning attempts from legitimate contributor noise.

T1037 is structurally identical to T1547 from a deception standpoint: a post-compromise, intra-host write operation. The attacker drops a script into an initialization location (init.d, rc.d, Windows logon script paths, macOS login hooks) on a machine they already control. There is no external client asset in the technique's execution path. T1037.003 (Network Logon Script) was examined separately — it targets a network share (SYSVOL in AD environments), which is a defender-controlled asset, but the attacker's action is still a write: they add their malicious script to the share rather than interacting with existing scripts. A honeypot VM observes T1037 activity but that is endpoint telemetry, not infrastructure deception. Prior analyses scoring this Yes conflated observation on a generic honeypot with fabricating a specific decoy asset that the technique targets.

T1053 is an action the attacker performs — creating or modifying scheduled tasks (Windows Task Scheduler, cron, systemd timers, container orchestration jobs) on a host they already control. The technique is the mechanism of execution and persistence, not the targeting of a specific asset a defender can fabricate. There is no client asset to place in the path of an attacker creating a scheduled task; the action is performed on infrastructure the attacker already owns.

Decoy accounts (honey accounts, honeytoken credentials, decoy SSH keys, fake service accounts) are fabricated technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure — AD, cloud IAM, SSH authorized_keys — that are passive and fully instrumented. Feasibility is Yes: the asset is well-established in practice and straightforward to deploy. Interaction is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the decoy credential must first be acquired before it can be used; interaction depends on placement strategy (breadcrumb in a config file, exposed in a compromised endpoint) rather than being self-attracting like a public-facing service. Intelligence yield is high: authentication metadata, source IP, timing patterns, targeted service, and post-authentication behavior if the account grants access to a decoy environment. Malice fidelity is Yes: no legitimate user knows about or has reason to use a fabricated account; false positives are limited to controlled security testing scenarios and are operationally manageable.

**Deception Utility:** High

The technique targets client assets that a defender can fully fabricate and instrument: honeypot AD accounts, decoy Linux hosts with planted SSH authorized_keys files, fake cloud IAM service principals, dummy Kubernetes role bindings, and decoy domain group memberships are all fabricatable and fully under defender control. Interaction is Mostly No because T1098 is post-compromise persistence — the attacker must first compromise a host or cloud environment, then discover the decoy account during enumeration, then choose to manipulate it over real accounts. On a realistic full decoy VM, an attacker following standard TTPs will attempt account manipulation as part of their normal playbook. On mixed real/decoy infrastructure, the attacker must encounter and prioritize the decoy account, which depends on positioning and is not a direct consequence of the technique. The dependency on prior discovery and the attacker's natural preference for high-value real accounts makes interaction possible but not expected. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the observable data is concrete and attribution-rich — which account was manipulated, which sub-technique was used (SSH key added, cloud credential created, group membership modified), tooling signatures (Mimikatz, native OS commands, cloud CLI), commands executed, timing, and the artifact itself as a concrete IOC. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes because deliberate account manipulation is not an accidental or routine action; the narrow false positive risk comes from legitimate IT automation (Ansible, Puppet, SCIM provisioning) or privileged administrators performing account maintenance on decoy accounts seeded in real infrastructure, both of which are identifiable by user attribution and change management context.

**Deception Utility:** Medium

T1112 is overwhelmingly a post-compromise, intra-host write operation: the attacker modifies the Windows Registry on a system they already control to store payloads, configure malware, disable security tools, or establish persistence. Two deception angles were examined and rejected. First, the remote Registry lateral movement scenario — T1112 can be used to modify the registry of a remote system via the Remote Registry service, making a decoy Windows host with Remote Registry enabled a candidate asset. This was rejected because the draw is the Windows host itself (reachable via credentials and network access), not the Registry service specifically; detection belongs to the credential use and lateral movement steps, not to a decoy asset specific to T1112. Second, a monitored honeytoken registry key was considered — a key that triggers an alert if modified. This was rejected because attackers write to keys that serve their operational purpose (C2 config storage, defense disablement, persistence locations); they do not interact with pre-planted neutral keys. The procedure example set, spanning hundreds of malware families and threat groups, shows no pattern that a defender could anticipate and position a specific decoy against.

Decoy remote access services (fake VPN endpoints, honeypot RDP/SSH servers, fake OWA portals, exposed Docker/Kubernetes APIs) are technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure that sit directly in the path of this technique. Exposed remote services are hit constantly by opportunistic brute-forcers and credential stuffers without requiring prior discovery. Intelligence yield is high: credential sets in circulation, brute force tooling, password spray patterns, and post-authentication attacker behavior. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes due to asset-type variance — generic SSH/RDP endpoints attract scanner noise, while internal-looking or specialized services (fake OWA, decoy VPN) have higher signal.

**Deception Utility:** High

T1136 is a creation operation: the attacker adds a new account to a local system, domain, or cloud tenant they already control. There is no pre-existing client asset for the defender to fabricate that the attacker will target. This is the structural inverse of T1098 (Account Manipulation), which targets existing accounts and can be countered with decoy accounts planted in the attacker's path. In T1136 the attacker bypasses any pre-planted asset entirely and creates their own entry. Canary accounts do not apply: a canary works when an attacker accesses or modifies something pre-positioned; here the attacker never touches existing accounts. A decoy AD domain or cloud tenant would observe account creation but that is generic post-compromise detection on a honeypot infrastructure, not a decoy asset specific to T1136.

T1137 covers post-compromise modification of Microsoft Office startup mechanisms — replacing VbaProject.OTM, installing malicious add-ins, setting Outlook rules or forms, or abusing the Office Test registry key — on a host or account the attacker already controls. The structure is identical to T1547 from a deception standpoint: a write operation performed after compromise with no external client asset in the technique's path. The Outlook-specific sub-techniques (T1137.003 Outlook Forms, T1137.005 Outlook Rules) were examined as candidates: a honeypot Exchange/M365 mailbox is a fabricatable asset, but the attacker must already hold valid credentials to reach it, and the persistence mechanism is installed on account infrastructure already under attacker control. Any observation would be generic post-compromise detection on a honeypot account, not a decoy asset specific to T1137.

T1176 covers two vectors: installing malicious browser or IDE extensions via social engineering (publishing in a marketplace and tricking users into installing), or direct installation by an attacker already on a compromised host. Neither has a fabricatable client asset in the technique's path. The social engineering vector targets user behavior, not infrastructure — the same reason T1204 (User Execution) is No. The direct installation vector is post-compromise and intra-host with no external asset to pre-plant. A fake developer persona publishing a decoy extension in a marketplace was considered but rejected: it falls outside the passive decoy framework and constitutes active adversary engagement rather than a fabricated client asset.

T1197 is a post-compromise, intra-host technique. The attacker invokes the BITS service locally on a machine they already control to download payloads, establish persistent callbacks, or exfiltrate data. In every usage pattern, the attacker specifies and controls the remote endpoint — BITS downloads from attacker-owned C2 infrastructure and uploads to attacker-owned destinations. There is no external client asset that the attacker targets using BITS that a defender could fabricate and position. Candidate decoys from prior analysis were found to be misclassified: "decoy BITS jobs" conflate endpoint telemetry with deception (BITS jobs are local and cannot be planted for an attacker to discover); "sinkhole URLs" are C2 interception infrastructure, not fabricated client assets. The technique is detectable via endpoint logging but offers no deception surface.

Traffic signaling hides attacker implants behind magic packets, port-knocking sequences, or secret strings. The implant is installed by the attacker on systems they have compromised; the attacker then signals it from the outside using a sequence only they know. There is no defender-positionable asset that mimics this technique: the listener is the attacker's own backdoor on an attacker-controlled compromised system, not a client asset a defender can fabricate. Evaluated under TA0005 (Defense Evasion); score applies equally here.

T1505 is a post-compromise write operation: the attacker installs a malicious server-side component — web shell, SQL stored procedure, Exchange transport agent, IIS module, Terminal Services DLL, or ESXi VIB — on a server they have already compromised. All six sub-techniques follow the same creation pattern: the attacker drops their own component rather than targeting a pre-existing one. This is structurally identical to T1136 (Create Account): the attacker bypasses any pre-planted asset and creates their own. The decoy asset is a fabricated internal image registry (AWS ECR, GCP Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry, or a private Docker registry) positioned as a plausible secondary or environment-scoped registry within the organization's cloud infrastructure. Feasibility is Mostly No because the registry itself is trivial to create, but convincing interaction requires a multi-registry enterprise environment where the decoy blends in; in single-registry environments the decoy is immediately identifiable. Interaction is Mostly No because the attacker must enumerate the cloud environment, find the decoy registry among real ones, and choose to push their backdoored image there rather than to a real registry — this requires a strong deception narrative and defender-directed positioning rather than being a natural consequence of following the technique. A decoy image pre-planted within the real registry was considered but rejected: T1525 is a push operation and the attacker would not interact with an existing image. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes — a decoy registry in a multi-registry environment could receive accidental pushes from developers or misconfigured CI/CD pipelines, which are identifiable by credential attribution and image naming but represent a real false positive class.

T1547 is a post-compromise, intra-host write operation. The attacker adds their own persistence entry to startup locations — registry run keys, startup folders, Winlogon configuration, kernel modules — on a machine they already control. There is no external client asset that the attacker targets. Honeytoken entries placed in startup locations were considered but rejected: T1547 is a write operation and the attacker adds new entries rather than interacting with existing ones. The technique is detectable via endpoint telemetry but presents no deception surface.

T1554 is a post-compromise, intra-host write operation: the attacker replaces or patches legitimate binaries on a machine they already control. There is no external client asset in the technique's execution path. The procedure examples show a strong pattern of VPN appliance targeting (Ivanti Connect Secure, Pulse Secure, FortiGate), which makes a decoy VPN appliance the closest candidate — it is a fabricatable asset and an actively sought target class. However, binary replacement is what the attacker does after compromising the device, not what draws them to it; initial access to a VPN appliance is T1190, not T1554. A honeypot appliance would observe T1554 activity but that is post-compromise detection, not a decoy asset specific to this technique. Canary binaries were considered but rejected: T1554 replaces the binary entirely, leaving no honeytoken in the execution path.

T1556 covers post-compromise modification of authentication mechanisms — LSASS/SAM on Windows, PAM on Unix, authentication plugins on macOS, network device AAA processes, MFA configurations, and cloud conditional access policies. In every sub-technique the attacker modifies auth infrastructure on a system they already control. The closest decoy candidates examined were a honeypot Cisco device (T1556.004) and a decoy Azure AD Connect server (T1556.007) — both are fabricatable assets — but both were rejected on the same grounds as T1554: T1556 is what happens after compromise, not what draws the attacker. A honeypot network device would observe auth modification activity, but the detection belongs to the initial access technique (T1133/T1190) that provided entry, not to a decoy asset specific to T1556. There is no pre-existing client asset in the path of this technique that a defender can fabricate and position.

T1574 covers 12 sub-techniques where the attacker places a malicious payload in a location the OS will find before the legitimate one — DLL hijacking, dylib hijacking, path interception, services permissions weaknesses, dynamic linker hijacking, and others. The deception angle examined was pre-planting a monitored decoy DLL in a known hijackable search-order location. This was rejected: the attacker places their own payload rather than interacting with an existing one, and a pre-planted decoy would be overwritten or bypassed. Occupying a hijackable slot with a monitored DLL is a mitigation strategy, not a deception asset. The scenario requires the defender to correctly anticipate the exact DLL slot the attacker will target, which is operationally highly constrained and not a natural consequence of the attacker following the technique.

T1653 is a post-compromise, intra-host configuration change: the attacker modifies power settings (via powercfg, lock screen timeout, hibernate settings) or deletes shutdown files on a host they already control to prevent the system from entering a dormant state. There is no external client asset in the technique's path. The ArcaneDoor/Line Runner procedure examples introduce a reboot-trigger angle — exploiting CVE-2024-20353 to force a Cisco ASA to reboot and load an implant — but the exploitation that draws the attacker to the device is T1190, not T1653; T1653 here describes the reboot-triggered implant loading mechanism, which is post-compromise behavior on a device already under attacker control. No fabricatable client asset exists specific to this technique.

T1668 describes a meta-behavior: the attacker hardens the compromised environment against competitors by patching vulnerabilities, disabling services, stripping account privileges, or removing other malware. The targets of these actions are real environment components, not specific assets a defender can fabricate and position in the technique's path. Candidate decoys examined and rejected: fake vulnerable services would not be targeted (attackers close real exposure vectors); planted malware artifacts could function as tripwires but require the attacker to actively hunt competing malware rather than simply harden their position; decoy accounts with fake privileges would be bypassed in favor of real lateral movement accounts. The technique has no procedure examples in ATT&CK, making it difficult to anchor to specific targeted assets. No passive deception surface exists.

The decoy asset is a fabricated SaaS tenant (M365, Google Workspace, or Salesforce org) positioned as a convincing subsidiary, test environment, or acquired-company tenant within the organization's cloud footprint. Feasibility is Mostly No because the asset itself is straightforward to create — spinning up a tenant is low-cost — but making it convincing enough to attract a targeted attacker requires a realistic deception narrative: plausible domain, realistic user accounts, existing OAuth integrations, and a discoverable cross-tenant trust relationship. Without this investment the decoy is inert. Interaction is Mostly No because the scenario requires an attacker who is enumerating cross-tenant relationships, which is sophisticated behavior not reflected in the limited procedure examples; most T1671 activity targets the primary compromised tenant directly. Azure AD and Google Workspace tenants are discoverable via domain probing and B2B trust enumeration, so a well-positioned decoy tenant is findable, but the attacker must be doing that level of cloud reconnaissance. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: cloud audit logs (Azure AD Unified Audit Log, Google Workspace Admin audit) capture the app registration, permissions requested, service principal created, consenting account identity, source IP, and any subsequent API calls — structured, tamper-resistant, and attribution-rich. Malice fidelity is Yes because a purpose-built decoy tenant has no real users or legitimate workflows; no IT process, developer, or automation has reason to register OAuth applications in it. Any app registration not from the defender's own initial setup is definitively malicious. FPs that are common in real tenants (user consent, IT admin registrations, automated service principal creation) do not apply to a controlled decoy environment.

**Deception Utility:** Medium

T1037 is structurally identical to T1547 from a deception standpoint: a post-compromise, intra-host write operation. The attacker drops a script into an initialization location (init.d, rc.d, Windows logon script paths, macOS login hooks) on a machine they already control. There is no external client asset in the technique's execution path. T1037.003 (Network Logon Script) was examined separately — it targets a network share (SYSVOL in AD environments), which is a defender-controlled asset, but the attacker's action is still a write: they add their malicious script to the share rather than interacting with existing scripts. A honeypot VM observes T1037 activity but that is endpoint telemetry, not infrastructure deception. Prior analyses scoring this Yes conflated observation on a generic honeypot with fabricating a specific decoy asset that the technique targets.

T1053 is an action the attacker performs — creating or modifying scheduled tasks (Windows Task Scheduler, cron, systemd timers, container orchestration jobs) on a host they already control. The technique is the mechanism of execution and persistence, not the targeting of a specific asset a defender can fabricate. There is no client asset to place in the path of an attacker creating a scheduled task; the action is performed on infrastructure the attacker already owns.

T1055 covers 12 sub-techniques for injecting attacker-controlled code into the address space of a running legitimate process. The honey process angle was examined and rejected on two independent grounds. First, the feasibility problem mirrors T1134: a running process is an actively maintained runtime object rather than a passively positioned static artifact, and detecting injection API calls (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread, ptrace) requires EDR instrumentation rather than a passive decoy revealing itself through interaction. Second, and more decisively, attackers select injection targets based on operational criteria — blending in with legitimate traffic, accessing specific memory or privileges, reaching network resources. They consistently target well-known system processes (explorer.exe, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, browser processes) and would actively bypass a planted fake process in favor of real ones. A fabricated process offers no blending value, wrong privilege context, and no operational utility to the attacker. Interaction with a honey process is not a natural consequence of following this technique.

T1068 covers exploitation of software vulnerabilities in OS components, kernel, drivers, and services to gain elevated privileges, including the BYOVD (Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver) pattern. The technique targets real software bugs, not static configuration artifacts a defender can fabricate and plant. Attackers bring known exploits and fire them at components they assume are present — the kernel, common drivers, well-known services — rather than discovering planted artifacts through enumeration. The planted vulnerable service angle was examined and rejected: deploying old vulnerable software exposes real software, not a fabricated artifact, and the draw to that service belongs to Discovery techniques rather than a T1068-specific decoy. BYOVD removes any defender-planted asset from the path entirely — the attacker supplies the vulnerable driver themselves. Unlike misconfigurations (sudoers entries, setuid binaries, mock docker sockets) which are static artifacts self-revealing through enumeration, software vulnerabilities have no equivalent planted artifact that reveals itself through attacker interaction. Detection of T1068 requires kernel-level or process-level monitoring, not a passive decoy.

Decoy accounts (honey accounts, honeytoken credentials, decoy SSH keys, fake service accounts) are fabricated technical entities on defender-controlled infrastructure — AD, cloud IAM, SSH authorized_keys — that are passive and fully instrumented. Feasibility is Yes: the asset is well-established in practice and straightforward to deploy. Interaction is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the decoy credential must first be acquired before it can be used; interaction depends on placement strategy (breadcrumb in a config file, exposed in a compromised endpoint) rather than being self-attracting like a public-facing service. Intelligence yield is high: authentication metadata, source IP, timing patterns, targeted service, and post-authentication behavior if the account grants access to a decoy environment. Malice fidelity is Yes: no legitimate user knows about or has reason to use a fabricated account; false positives are limited to controlled security testing scenarios and are operationally manageable.

**Deception Utility:** High

The technique targets client assets that a defender can fully fabricate and instrument: honeypot AD accounts, decoy Linux hosts with planted SSH authorized_keys files, fake cloud IAM service principals, dummy Kubernetes role bindings, and decoy domain group memberships are all fabricatable and fully under defender control. Interaction is Mostly No because T1098 is post-compromise persistence — the attacker must first compromise a host or cloud environment, then discover the decoy account during enumeration, then choose to manipulate it over real accounts. On a realistic full decoy VM, an attacker following standard TTPs will attempt account manipulation as part of their normal playbook. On mixed real/decoy infrastructure, the attacker must encounter and prioritize the decoy account, which depends on positioning and is not a direct consequence of the technique. The dependency on prior discovery and the attacker's natural preference for high-value real accounts makes interaction possible but not expected. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the observable data is concrete and attribution-rich — which account was manipulated, which sub-technique was used (SSH key added, cloud credential created, group membership modified), tooling signatures (Mimikatz, native OS commands, cloud CLI), commands executed, timing, and the artifact itself as a concrete IOC. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes because deliberate account manipulation is not an accidental or routine action; the narrow false positive risk comes from legitimate IT automation (Ansible, Puppet, SCIM provisioning) or privileged administrators performing account maintenance on decoy accounts seeded in real infrastructure, both of which are identifiable by user attribution and change management context.

**Deception Utility:** Medium

T1134 covers five sub-techniques for stealing and manipulating Windows access tokens on a host the attacker already controls. The "honey process" angle was examined — running a background process under a honey account so its token is available in memory for attackers enumerating processes. This was rejected on two grounds. First, the deceptive value derives from the account identity (T1078), not from a technique-specific fabricated artifact; any detection of credential use following token theft belongs to T1078, not T1134. Second, a running process is an actively maintained runtime object, not a passively positioned static artifact — detecting the T1134 action (OpenProcessToken, DuplicateTokenEx API calls) requires EDR instrumentation rather than the decoy being self-revealing through interaction. This distinguishes it from static planted artifacts like sudoers entries or setuid binaries, which produce observable events when acted on without requiring active API monitoring. No fabricatable passive decoy asset sits in the execution path of this technique.

Honey GPOs and decoy federation trust objects are fabricatable AD and cloud artifacts fully under defender control. A GPO named to suggest governance of high-value targets (e.g., "SQL-Admins-Policy", "C-Suite-Workstation-Security") or a decoy federation trust object styled as a legacy "M&A staging" relationship are realistic and cheap to deploy. Feasibility is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the deception only works for the subset of attackers who enumerate and modify existing policy objects rather than creating new ones — a real but not dominant attacker pattern. Interaction is Mostly No: the attacker must have domain admin privileges, enumerate existing GPOs or trust objects, and choose the honey object over real ones; many attackers create new GPOs rather than modifying existing ones, limiting interaction probability. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the modification is concrete and attribution-rich, revealing the account used, the specific changes made, tooling, and timing. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because on real mixed infrastructure a honey GPO could be touched by GPO management tooling, bulk audit scripts, or an administrator unaware of the decoy — false positives are narrow but operationally plausible.

Interaction is Mostly Yes: attackers enumerating for escape paths (`find / -name docker.sock`, checking for privileged mounts, inspecting `/proc`) will encounter these artifacts as a natural post-compromise step in containerized environments, and will attempt to use them. Prior access to the server is required but does not affect the technique-specific evaluation. Intelligence yield is Yes: the escape attempt reveals the specific method and tooling used (e.g., exploit code for kernel vulnerabilities, Docker API calls), a strong sophistication marker that distinguishes an opportunistic bot from an operator with container internals knowledge. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because on a real server a legitimate container management tool or misconfigured deployment pipeline could inadvertently communicate with a mock socket — false positives are narrow but operationally plausible.

T1006 targets OS-managed logical volumes and shadow copies — system constructs tied to actual disk layout that a defender cannot independently fabricate or position as a decoy. There is no standalone "fake volume" artifact a defender can deploy that would look convincing to an attacker targeting known system volumes (e.g., C: or DC shadow copies for NTDS.dit extraction). Planting canary data inside real shadow copies is possible but the detection signal fires at credential use downstream, not at the point of volume access — that is T1003 deception, not T1006 deception. No feasible decoy asset exists for this technique.

A rootkit is a capability an attacker deploys on a host they have already compromised, not a client asset a defender owns or positions. It operates by hooking OS API calls to hide processes, files, and network connections. There is no static artifact a defender can fabricate and expose as a decoy: no service to impersonate, no file or credential to plant, no network endpoint to advertise. Mimicking this technique would require the defender to already have a compromised host with rootkit-like behavior, which inverts the deception model entirely. Feasibility is No.

The technique describes what attackers do to their own files and code before or during delivery — encoding, encrypting, packing, steganography. There is no defender-side artifact to fabricate. A honey file that resembles an obfuscated payload could be placed on a share or endpoint, but the deception value would come from file access, not from mimicking obfuscation as a technique. The 17 sub-techniques all describe attacker-side transformations applied to attacker-controlled content. Feasibility is No.

However, the attacker does not seek these out because of what they mimic; they clear whatever artifacts exist on the host. Any detection from a honey log or fake registry key being deleted is incidental and belongs to file or registry access monitoring, not to a deception asset mimicking this technique. Without a full honeypot OS, there is no fabricatable client asset specific to this technique. Feasibility is No.

T1112 is overwhelmingly a post-compromise, intra-host write operation: the attacker modifies the Windows Registry on a system they already control to store payloads, configure malware, disable security tools, or establish persistence. Two deception angles were examined and rejected. First, the remote Registry lateral movement scenario — T1112 can be used to modify the registry of a remote system via the Remote Registry service, making a decoy Windows host with Remote Registry enabled a candidate asset. This was rejected because the draw is the Windows host itself (reachable via credentials and network access), not the Registry service specifically; detection belongs to the credential use and lateral movement steps, not to a decoy asset specific to T1112. Second, a monitored honeytoken registry key was considered — a key that triggers an alert if modified. This was rejected because attackers write to keys that serve their operational purpose (C2 config storage, defense disablement, persistence locations); they do not interact with pre-planted neutral keys. The procedure example set, spanning hundreds of malware families and threat groups, shows no pattern that a defender could anticipate and position a specific decoy against.

Attackers invoke specific trusted tools — MSBuild, ClickOnce, JamPlus — from their known, fixed, signed paths to bypass application controls. Two factors rule out a viable decoy. First, attackers using these tools have already decided on a specific binary and invoke it by its canonical path; a fake copy in a non-standard location would not be invoked. Second, instrumenting or replacing the real tool on developer machines would break legitimate build workflows, making decoy deployment operationally unsafe. The "decoy in non-standard path" logic that applied to T1218 and T1216 does not transfer here because the attacker's trust in these tools is path-dependent.

The decoding or deobfuscation of payloads occurs within the malware itself or via attacker-controlled tooling (e.g., certutil, PowerShell, custom decryption routines). No client asset is targeted or interacted with during this process. There is nothing for a defender to fabricate as a decoy. The technique is self-contained within the attacker's toolchain and offers no interaction surface for deception.

T1197 is a post-compromise, intra-host technique. The attacker invokes the BITS service locally on a machine they already control to download payloads, establish persistent callbacks, or exfiltrate data. In every usage pattern, the attacker specifies and controls the remote endpoint — BITS downloads from attacker-owned C2 infrastructure and uploads to attacker-owned destinations. There is no external client asset that the attacker targets using BITS that a defender could fabricate and position. Candidate decoys from prior analysis were found to be misclassified: "decoy BITS jobs" conflate endpoint telemetry with deception (BITS jobs are local and cannot be planted for an attacker to discover); "sinkhole URLs" are C2 interception infrastructure, not fabricated client assets. Indirect Command Execution abuses legitimate Windows utilities already present on the system (Forfiles, pcalua.exe, WSL, ssh.exe) to run commands without invoking cmd.exe directly. The attacker is not seeking out a planted asset — they leverage what is natively available. A honey binary named after one of these utilities could be planted, but the real utilities already exist on Windows hosts and the attacker would use those instead. Monitoring execution of these binaries is a detection problem, not a deception one. Feasibility is No.

Traffic signaling hides attacker implants behind magic packets, port-knocking sequences, or secret strings. The implant is installed by the attacker on systems they have compromised; the attacker then signals it from the outside using a sequence only they know. There is no defender-positionable asset that mimics this technique: the listener is the attacker's own backdoor on an attacker-controlled compromised system, not a client asset a defender can fabricate. An attacker would never probe a random system for a traffic-signaled backdoor they did not install — they only signal hosts where their own implant is already running.

The attacker registers the rogue Domain Controller — it is their object, created by their action. The defender has no role in positioning a DC that an attacker would interact with. While a honey DC could theoretically be registered by a defender to monitor replication activity, the technique describes the attacker performing the registration, not seeking out an existing DC to abuse. Feasibility is No.

This technique targets real defensive software — AV, EDR, OS components, cloud infrastructure — exploiting vulnerabilities in those tools to disable or circumvent them. A decoy security agent (a process mimicking an EDR or AV) could be fabricated and made visible to enumeration, but the technique requires the attacker to exploit an actual vulnerability in that software. A fake process provides no real attack surface; exploitation attempts would fail or behave unexpectedly. The detection opportunity from a visible decoy security process belongs to Security Software Discovery (T1518), not to this technique. LLM-backed simulation of a vulnerable security agent was considered but rejected: exploitation of security software is largely in-process and local (kernel objects, IPC, driver interfaces), not network-facing interactions an LLM could realistically simulate. Feasibility is No.

Same reasoning as T1218. A decoy script named after a trusted Microsoft script (e.g., PubPrn.vbs, SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs) placed in a non-standard path is a fabricatable client asset. The decoy does not need to be signed — signing is what makes the real script trusted by the OS, not what makes a lure attractive to an attacker referencing it by path. Feasibility is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the decoy is only operationally viable on a honey host or honey share, not on production systems where the real scripts already exist. Interaction is Mostly No for the same reason. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes: no legitimate process references a non-standard copy of these scripts.

**Deception Utility:** Low

A fake LOLBin — a monitored executable named after a trusted Windows binary (rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe) placed in a non-standard path such as a honey share or honey host — is a fabricatable client asset. Feasibility is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the decoy is only operationally viable outside a production system context; the real System32 binaries cannot be replaced without breaking legitimate software. Interaction is Mostly No: attackers default to real System32 binaries and would only reach the decoy if operating on a honey host or if referencing the binary from a non-standard path. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the attacker reveals their tooling, execution method, payload, and C2 parameters. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes: a monitored fake binary in a non-standard location has no legitimate use; the narrow false positive risk comes from misconfigured scripts or tooling that references non-standard paths.

**Deception Utility:** Low

**Deception Utility:** Low

T1220 uses XSL files to proxy execution via msxsl.exe or wmic /FORMAT, bypassing application controls. A decoy XSL file placed on a honey host or share represents a fabricatable client asset in the post-initial-access scenario, where an attacker might find and reference a local XSL file. However, msxsl.exe is not installed by default — attackers typically drop it themselves and bring their own XSL payload, making it unlikely they would hunt for existing XSL files on a compromised system. The wmic /FORMAT variant could reference a local file, creating a narrow interaction window. Feasibility is Mostly No rather than No because the post-initial-access scenario is technically possible, following the same logic as T1216. If a decoy XSL file is executed, the intelligence is clear (source, timing, execution context) and the malice fidelity is high — no legitimate process executes a non-standard XSL file via these tools.

**Deception Utility:** Low

T1221 covers two distinct scenarios. In the phishing delivery scenario, the attacker crafts a malicious document and sends it to a victim — the defender has no asset to position and no decoy is possible. In the post-initial-access scenario, the attacker finds and modifies existing template files (e.g., Office templates, RTF files) to inject remote URLs, either to fetch payloads or force authentication from other users. In this second scenario, decoy template files placed on a compromised system or honey share represent a fabricatable client asset. However, the technique requires the attacker to specifically seek out and modify template files, which is a specialized behavior not universal across intrusions.

If an attacker does interact with a decoy template file, the intelligence is clear and actionable (attacker active on that system, modification confirmed) and the malice fidelity is high — no legitimate user injects remote URLs into template files.

This technique is an action performed on existing files and directories on a host the attacker already controls — modifying ACLs or ownership to bypass access controls. The attacker is not seeking out a planted asset; they are operating on real system objects. A honey file or directory with specific permissions could be positioned on a host, but any detection from an attacker accessing or modifying it comes from file access monitoring, not from a deception asset mimicking this technique. A full honeypot system could observe the behavior, but that is an environment-level deception, not a fabricatable client asset in the framework's sense. Feasibility is No.

Execution guardrails are logic baked into the attacker's payload — conditions the malware checks before proceeding (hostname, domain name, file path, language setting, mutex, IP address). The defender has no role in that decision chain. The only conceivable angle is a defender who knows the specific guardrail conditions and engineers a honey environment to satisfy them, triggering payload execution for observation. That is not mimicking the technique as a decoy but a threat-intel-driven sandbox setup, and not a generalizable deception asset. Feasibility is No.

Honey GPOs and decoy federation trust objects are fabricatable AD and cloud artifacts fully under defender control. A GPO named to suggest governance of high-value targets (e.g., "SQL-Admins-Policy", "C-Suite-Workstation-Security") or a decoy federation trust object styled as a legacy "M&A staging" relationship are realistic and cheap to deploy. Feasibility is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because the deception only works for the subset of attackers who enumerate and modify existing policy objects rather than creating new ones — a real but not dominant attacker pattern. Interaction is Mostly No: the attacker must have domain admin privileges, enumerate existing GPOs or trust objects, and choose the honey object over real ones; many attackers create new GPOs rather than modifying existing ones, limiting interaction probability. Intelligence yield is Yes when interaction occurs: the modification is concrete and attribution-rich, revealing the account used, the specific changes made, tooling, and timing. Malice fidelity is Mostly Yes rather than Yes because on real mixed infrastructure a honey GPO could be touched by GPO management tooling, bulk audit scripts, or an administrator unaware of the decoy — false positives are narrow but operationally plausible.

**Deception Utility:** Medium

T1497 is an intra-process malware behavior: the attacker's code checks local system artifacts (VM indicators, user activity, timing) to determine whether it is running in an analysis environment, then alters execution accordingly. All checks are internal to the malware and operate against the local environment. There is no defender-positionable client asset to fabricate. Anti-anti-VM techniques (making a real system appear non-virtualized) are a malware analysis approach, not an Intel-Deception Matrix deception asset.

T1535 is a purely attacker-side action: the attacker provisions their own resources in a cloud region the organization does not monitor, using a compromised account. There is no defender-positionable client asset to fabricate. The technique is about the attacker's choice of infrastructure placement, not about interacting with defender-controlled assets.

T1542 covers post-compromise modification of pre-OS boot mechanisms — BIOS/UEFI firmware, component firmware, MBR/VBR bootkits, Cisco ROMMON, and TFTP boot configuration — on devices the attacker has already compromised. There is no external client asset in the technique's path. The TFTP Boot sub-technique (T1542.005) was examined separately: the attacker configures a Cisco device to fetch firmware from an attacker-controlled TFTP server, so the TFTP server is attacker infrastructure, not a defender-fabricatable asset. A honeypot Cisco router or network device could observe ROMMON or firmware modification post-compromise, but the draw to the device is T1190, not T1542. No fabricatable client asset exists specific to this technique.

T1548 describes abusing elevation control mechanisms (UAC, sudo, setuid, elevated execution prompts, TCC manipulation, temporary cloud access). These are OS-level control mechanisms that the attacker exploits on their foothold. The defender cannot fabricate the elevation control mechanism itself as a decoy asset. While individual sub-techniques like sudo rules or setuid binaries could theoretically be planted, the technique as a whole does not involve the attacker targeting a pre-existing client asset that a defender can mimic.

**Deception Utility:** High

The client assets here are the authentication materials themselves: NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, OAuth tokens, and session cookies. A defender can fabricate all of these as honey credentials — a fake hash planted in memory on a honey endpoint, a honey OAuth token in a config file, a decoy Kerberos ticket. These are fully fabricatable and require no real authentication infrastructure. The decoy is specifically alternate authentication material (not a plaintext password), so when an attacker steals and uses it, the authentication event reveals the technique in use: Pass the Hash shows NTLM relay behavior, Pass the Ticket shows Kerberos ticket usage, token replay shows OAuth flow. This technique-specific intelligence is only available if the decoy was planted as alternate auth material. Interaction is Yes because an attacker who steals a credential will use it — the usage attempt follows naturally from the theft. Intel yield and malice fidelity are both high: the authentication event is unambiguous and no legitimate user would use a fabricated credential.

Subvert Trust Controls covers 6 sub-techniques all targeting OS and security trust mechanisms — Gatekeeper bypass, code signing, root certificate installation, Mark-of-the-Web bypass, trust provider hijacking. The attacker operates on system trust infrastructure they have already accessed; they are not seeking out a planted defender asset. There is nothing to fabricate as a decoy. Feasibility is No.

T1556 covers post-compromise modification of authentication mechanisms — LSASS/SAM on Windows, PAM on Unix, authentication plugins on macOS, network device AAA processes, MFA configurations, and cloud conditional access policies. In every sub-technique the attacker modifies auth infrastructure on a system they already control. The closest decoy candidates examined were a honeypot Cisco device (T1556.004) and a decoy Azure AD Connect server (T1556.007) — both are fabricatable assets — but both were rejected on the same grounds as T1554: T1556 is what happens after compromise, not what draws the attacker. A honeypot network device would observe auth modification activity, but the detection belongs to the initial access technique (T1133/T1190) that provided entry, not to a decoy asset specific to T1556. There is no pre-existing client asset in the path of this technique that a defender can fabricate and position.

Impair Defenses targets real defensive infrastructure — disabling AV tools, turning off event logging, modifying firewall rules, disabling cloud audit logs. The attacker operates on components of the environment they have already compromised, not seeking out a planted artifact. T1562.011 (Spoof Security Alerting) is slightly different in character — the attacker generates fake alerts to mask activity — but it is still an attacker-side action with no defender decoy role. A decoy host with a monitored security stack could detect disable attempts, but that is environment-level deception rather than a fabricatable client asset. Feasibility is No.

Hide Artifacts covers 14 sub-techniques, all of which describe actions the attacker performs on their own artifacts to conceal them — hiding files, directories, users, windows, registry keys, file system regions, and process arguments. The defender has no role in that action chain. There is no planted asset an attacker seeks out; the attacker operates on objects they already control on a compromised host. Feasibility is No.

T1574 covers 12 sub-techniques where the attacker places a malicious payload in a location the OS will find before the legitimate one — DLL hijacking, dylib hijacking, path interception, services permissions weaknesses, dynamic linker hijacking, and others. The deception angle examined was pre-planting a monitored decoy DLL in a known hijackable search-order location. This was rejected: the attacker places their own payload rather than interacting with an existing one, and a pre-planted decoy would be overwritten or bypassed. Occupying a hijackable slot with a monitored DLL is a mitigation strategy, not a deception asset. The scenario requires the defender to correctly anticipate the exact DLL slot the attacker will target, which is operationally highly constrained and not a natural consequence of the attacker following the technique.

This technique describes actions an attacker performs after they already have cloud access — creating, deleting, modifying, or reverting compute instances and snapshots to evade defenses or erase evidence. A decoy cloud account could attract an attacker during initial access, but that is a credential or account-targeting technique, not this one. Once inside, the attacker manipulates infrastructure they find in the environment; any detection at that point comes from cloud audit logs (CloudTrail, etc.), not from a fabricated client asset mimicking this technique. Feasibility is No.

Network Boundary Bridging requires the attacker to have already compromised a perimeter device (router, firewall) and then reconfigure it to bypass network segmentation. This is post-access manipulation of network infrastructure the attacker controls — same pattern as T1601 and T1578. There is no fabricatable client asset a defender can position that an attacker would seek out to execute this technique. Feasibility is No.

T1600 involves compromising real network devices (routers, VPN appliances) to reduce key space or disable crypto hardware, weakening encryption on traffic passing through. The technique abuses real system features on already-compromised infrastructure. There is no fabricatable client asset a defender can position: the attacker modifies real devices they have already compromised, and no decoy network device would be interacted with as part of this technique.

Modify System Image targets embedded network devices (routers, switches) where the OS is a monolithic image. Attackers with access patch or downgrade that image in memory or storage to weaken defenses or add capabilities. This is post-access manipulation of device infrastructure the attacker already controls — same pattern as T1578 and T1666. There is no fabricatable client asset a defender can position that an attacker would seek out to execute this technique. Feasibility is No.
